To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the acid titration of streptococci reveals that intracellular ions are bound to internal cell constituents in different physical states and that the cell membrane acts as a barrier to their movement.

the cell membrane acts as a barrier to the diffusion of Mg2+, that Mg2+ can be displaced reversibly from intact cells by hydronum ions, and that the cell membrane becomes more permeable to hydronium and Mg2+ ions in acidic media.

the cell membrane of Streptococcusaerophilus acts as a barrier to the movement of ions between the intracellular and extracellular phases, that magnesium can be displaced reversibly from the cell membrane and from ribosomes, and that acidification of cells causes changes in the physical state of the cell membrane.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physical states of ions in bacterial cells, with special reference to their association with cell components.
the physical states of intracellular ions, the nature of the barriers which restrict their movements, and the mechanisms by which the barriers can be disrupted.
the physical states of intracellular ions in relation to the acid-base properties of the cell membrane, the cell walls, the ribosomes, and the protoplast membranes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
acid titrations of cells of Streptoccus faecalis and S. lactis revealed that nearly all intracellular K+ and Mg2+ ions could diffuse out of cells in association with small intracellular anions.
acidification causes the release of intracellular ions and the physical changes of cell membranes.

the intracellular magnesium of streptococci is associated with stable cell components which cannot diffuse into the medium, even in the presence of butanol damage, but can be displaced reversibly in acid media.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
acidification of the cytosol causes a decrease in membrane permeability and a loss of osmotic resistance, and this is due to a decrease in the net charge of the cell membrane.
intracellular Mg2+, but not K+, is firmly bound to stable cell constituents, and this binding is responsible for the acid resistance of cells in the pH range between 6 and 3.

the intracellular magnesium of intact cells of Streptoccocus faecalis is bound to carboxyl groups of ribosomes and cell wall polymers and to the surface of membranes, but that it is also bound to the surface of cell membranes and is thus not readily exchangeable with hydronium and other cations in acid media.
The main takeaway from our work is that
acid-base titrations can provide useful information about intracellular ions, but that the interpretation of such results must be done with caution.
the cell wall and membrane are the major sites of intracellular Mg2+.
the acid-base titrations of Streptococcussp., which have been used for decades, are actually measuring the acid-base titration of the cell wall and not the cell membrane.
